title: Lydia Gold Order
subject: Contracts
stem:
BARMATRIX Q# 14397 — Christian variation: 14397_lydia_gold_order

In a telephone conversation, Lydia, a maker of Christian jewelry, offered to buy 100 ounces of gold from Daniel's precious-metals company if delivery could be made within 10 days. Lydia did not specify a price, but the market price for 100 ounces of gold at the time of the conversation was approximately $65,000. Without otherwise responding, the company delivered the gold six days later. In the meantime, the gold-cross pendant line for which Lydia planned to use the gold was canceled by her retail buyer. Lydia therefore refused to accept delivery of the gold or to pay the $65,000 demanded by the company.

Is there an enforceable contract between Lydia and the company?
call: Is there an enforceable contract between Lydia and the company?

choices.A: No, because the parties did not agree on a price term.
choices.B: No, because the parties did not put their agreement in writing.
choices.C: Yes, because the absence of a price term does not defeat the formation of a valid contract for the sale of goods where the parties otherwise intended to form a contract.
choices.D: Yes, because the company relied on an implied promise to pay when it delivered the gold.

rightExplanation: B is correct. Gold Key: A contract for the sale of goods for $500 or more is unenforceable without a writing signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought — a perfectly formed oral deal above the threshold still cannot be enforced. This was a telephone deal for roughly $65,000 of gold, and Lydia never signed anything. Formation is not the problem: her offer invited acceptance by performance, and the company's six-day delivery likely accepted it; the missing price does not matter either, because the UCC supplies a reasonable price. The deal fails at the second gate — enforceability. Silver Key: "Is there an enforceable contract?" is a two-gate call — formation AND no defense; a "Yes" answer that recites a true formation rule still has to clear every defense, and a five-figure phone deal with nothing signed should send you hunting for one. No exception saves the company: Lydia refused the gold, so the goods were never received and accepted, no payment was made, the gold is ordinary market stock rather than specially manufactured goods, and no written confirmation was ever sent. The oral agreement is unenforceable against Lydia.

wrongExplanations.A: A reaches the right outcome for the wrong reason, and on the MBE the reason is part of the answer. Under the UCC, the parties' failure to agree on a price does not defeat formation: when the parties intend a contract and the price is left open, the price is simply a reasonable price at the time of delivery. The missing price term is a decoy. The real defect in this deal is the absence of a signed writing, not the absence of a number.
wrongExplanations.C: C is the dominant trap — 48% of students picked it, more than picked the key. Everything C says about the law is true: an open price term does not defeat formation of a sale-of-goods contract where the parties otherwise intended to contract. But C answers only the formation gate of a two-gate call. Gold Key: a contract for the sale of goods for $500 or more is unenforceable without a writing signed by the party to be charged — so a true formation rule cannot make this $65,000 oral deal enforceable. Silver Key: when the call asks "enforceable," a Yes-answer must survive every defense, not just formation; the moment you see a big-number phone deal and no signature anywhere in the stem, the defense hunt — not the price term — decides the question.
wrongExplanations.D: D dresses the seller's performance up as equity: the company "relied" by delivering, so fairness should bind Lydia. But Lydia refused to accept the gold. Gold Key: part performance saves an oral sale-of-goods contract only as to goods that have been received AND accepted (or paid for) — a delivery the buyer turns away satisfies nothing. Because the gold was never accepted, the company's delivery cannot substitute for the missing writing, and whether there was an implied promise to pay is irrelevant.

c3.label: A vs C
c3.text:
form a visible contradictory pair: both turn on the same stem fact (no price was specified) and assert opposite consequences — A says the missing price kills the deal, C says it doesn't. At most one can be true, and the pairing itself tells you the test-writer built the price term as a fought-over axis. The pair cannot be resolved at CUT without doctrine, so neither is cut here; the structure only flags them.
- D is wounded at CUT on a fairness tell plus a fact relation: "relied on an implied promise to pay when it delivered" is an equity appeal, and the stem shows Lydia refused the gold — D asks you to bind the buyer because the seller performed, when the stem says the performance was turned away. The full kill (part performance requires received-and-accepted goods) needs the Gold Key, so D is anchor-assisted, not structurally false.
- B survives: nothing in the stem contradicts it, and it is responsive to the enforceability call.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: B vs. C fight on a single axis: does answering the formation question (the open price term) answer the enforceability question? C wins the formation gate; B says there is a second gate. The splitting facts are "in a telephone conversation" plus "approximately $65,000" plus the total absence of any signed paper anywhere in the stem.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: The axis does not resolve from the stem alone; it takes the taught anchor. Gold Key: a contract for the sale of goods for $500 or more is unenforceable without a writing signed by the party to be charged, and refused goods are never "received and accepted." The $65,000 phone deal fails the writing requirement and no exception saves it. A falls with the same stroke (the open-price rule means A's stated reason is not the law), and D's reliance story cannot substitute for the writing. Residual answer: B.

studentScript: The call asks 'enforceable,' not 'formed' — two gates. A and C fight over the missing price; park the pair, price is the decoy. D begs fairness for a delivery Lydia turned away. That leaves B: a $65,000 deal made entirely by phone, and nobody signed anything. Gold Key: goods of $500 or more need a signed writing, and refused goods are never received and accepted. Pick B.

A.signal: A and C contradict each other on the same fact (no price was specified) — at most one is true, and the pair flags price as the decoy axis. Resolving which one falls takes the open-price anchor.
A.lawyer: UCC § 2-305(1): the parties can conclude a contract even though the price is not settled; if they intend a contract, the price is a reasonable price at the time for delivery. A invents a price-agreement requirement that Article 2 does not impose; the 'No' outcome is right but the stated reason is not the law.

B.signal: The only 'No' choice that points to something other than the flagged decoy axis. Once the two-gate Silver Key fires — formation AND no defense — B is the lone choice aimed at the defense gate.
B.lawyer: UCC § 2-201(1): a contract for the sale of goods for $500 or more is not enforceable absent a writing signed by the party to be charged. The deal was entirely oral, worth ~$65,000, and Lydia signed nothing. No § 2-201(3) exception applies: the goods were never received and accepted (she refused delivery), no payment was made, market gold is not specially manufactured, and there is no pleading admission; § 2-201(2)'s merchants' confirmation requires a writing and the company sent none.

C.signal: The call asks 'enforceable contract?' — a two-gate call. C answers only the formation gate (the open price term) and never speaks to any defense. The Silver Key wounds it; the full kill (the writing requirement) takes the Gold Key.
C.lawyer: C's rule statement is accurate (UCC § 2-305 — open price does not defeat formation), but the dispositive issue is the § 2-201 statute of frauds. Formation likely occurred (§ 2-206(1)(b): an offer to buy goods for prompt shipment invites acceptance by prompt shipment), yet the oral agreement remains unenforceable against Lydia for want of a signed writing.

D.signal: D is a fairness appeal — bind the buyer because the seller performed. The stem itself pushes back: Lydia refused the gold, so the 'reliance' D credits is a delivery that was turned away. The conclusive kill (part performance counts only for goods received AND accepted) takes the Gold Key.
D.lawyer: UCC § 2-201(3)(c) makes an oral contract enforceable only 'with respect to goods... which have been received and accepted' or paid for. Lydia accepted nothing and paid nothing, so the company's delivery cannot substitute for the writing; as the official explanation notes, whether there was an implied promise to pay is irrelevant once acceptance is absent.

remediation.title: Big phone deal, nothing signed
remediation.signal: A sale of goods at a four- or five-figure price is formed entirely by conversation, and the call asks whether the contract is enforceable.
remediation.studentMove: Run the two-gate call: park the decoy pair fighting over formation, then hunt the defense — who signed what?
remediation.tinyRule: Goods deals of $500 or more need a writing signed by the party being sued; refused goods are never 'received and accepted.'
remediation.trap: Crediting a true open-price formation rule as if formation were the only gate, or letting the seller's refused delivery 'equitably' bind the buyer.
